title: STUB: Term 3 Template Check
child_idea: This is a stub lesson used to prove the Term 2 template; it is not a lesson.

moe.note: STUB. Not a lesson: it exists only to exercise the Term 2 figure types, answer tokens, runner items and term-aware footers. Lesson 11 (Who Is Where?) replaces this file.

contest_moves: split a number into tens and ones
digit-clue puzzle (find the number from two clues)
objectives: Exercise every Term 2 figure type once in the workbook.
Exercise the runner: pictures, ordered boxes, list helpers, ordinals, templated choice.

remember: Ten and some more (11 to 19, then 20s and 30s)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and showing a number with fingers. Nothing from the holiday course is needed; if the child has done it, skip counting in 10s and bonds to 10 will feel familiar.
holiday_topics_revisited: Skip counting in 10s (Count with the Frog)
joining_cold.note: Lesson 1 is one of the hardest to miss in Term 1 (plan, section 2). A child who misses it watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 before Lesson 2.

child: About 50 small things of one kind: paper clips, dried pasta, buttons, lolly sticks or straws cut short
6 hair ties, small cups, paper rings or pieces of string (to hold a bundle), or draw rings on paper
The printed workbook (pages 1 to 5) and the kit page (tens bars and ones squares), already cut out by a grown-up
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
tutor: A slide deck and a tray of 30 lolly sticks or straws with three hair ties to show on camera if you wish
A timer slide or a visible clock
kit_pages: Stub: every Term 3 and 4 kit page
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought: everything can be found at home. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears.

timing.notes: Lesson 1 of the term has a 4-minute opening because it introduces the routine and the four inquirer rules. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.

sneak_peek.q1: Count the stars. Write how many. You may draw rings round groups to help.
sneak_peek.q2: Mei has 3 bundles of ten sticks and 4 single sticks. Ben has 34 sticks. Could they have the same number of sticks? Circle Yes or No. I know because ___.
sneak_peek.a2: Yes. 3 bundles of ten is 30, and 4 more is 34.

opening.say: If you are watching the recording: hello! Get a pencil, paper, your workbook and your things to bundle. Pause or rewind any time.
opening.action: Gather your workbook, pencil, paper and things to bundle. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Say the numbers out loud and show your fingers. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Say and show each answer before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

explore.say: Recording: pause now. Grab a handful, make bundles of ten, then build the numbers I call. Press play when you have tried.
explore.action: Pause. Grab and bundle, then build each number with your kit. Write what you find.

mini.say: Recording: keep watching and copy the examples. Rewind if you miss a step.
mini.action: Watch and copy the examples. Rewind any step you missed.

break.say: Recording: stand up and join in! Big jump for a ten, small hop for a one.
break.action: Stand up and jump the tens and hop the ones.

work.say: Recording: pause now and do workbook page 1. When you finish a page, press play to check it.
work.action: Pause. Do page 1, then play to check. Then page 2. Then choose a page to try.

talk.say: Recording: pause. Tell a grown-up your answer to the talk question, and say why.
talk.action: Pause. Explain your answer to someone at home, with a reason.

exit.say: Recording: pause and do the exit ticket on your own. Then press play to check it.
exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

look.say: Recording: pause and fill in your look-back box. You can pass.
look.action: Pause. Fill in the look-back box, or pass.

flex.say: Recording: well done for finishing! Show a grown-up one thing you found out.
flex.action: Show a grown-up your workbook and tell them one thing you found out.

lines.text: @rec

Hello, inquirers! Please stay muted unless I invite you to speak; give me a thumbs-up if you want to talk. Cameras on if you can, so I can see your page and hands. Cameras off is fine too. Pencil ready, and your things to bundle on the table.
This lesson is recorded so that a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and anyone's voice that is unmuted. You may mute and keep your camera off.
Here is our plan. A warm-up, two puzzles, then we explore with real things. Then I teach you a trick, we move, and you work in your workbook.
Four inquirer rules. Notice it: look closely. Test it: try it with real things. Explain why: say how you know. Mistakes help us: a guess is fine and you can always pass.
A shopkeeper has 47 pencils to count for a customer. Counting one by one is slow, and it is easy to lose count.
What could the shopkeeper do to count faster? Tell your screen or your grown-up.
Today we learn the shopkeeper's trick: bundles of ten.
If you can, greet each child by first name before you start the recording. While it runs, avoid names. Check that the page and hands can be seen, or ask the grown-up.

Lesson 1 only: show the routine slide for 20 seconds and name the phases; do not read the table. Say the recording notice in your own words: the recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted; children may mute and keep their camera off. Standing routine for every lesson: children are muted unless invited; for a group answer they say it quietly to their own room on a count of three.
@rec
Stand up if you can. We clap on every number. Count in tens with me: ten, twenty, thirty, all the way to one hundred.
Count in tens together, clapping, to 100. Then back from 100 to 0, whispering, with big hands on 50.
Fingers to ten. I say a number. Show me how many more fingers make ten.
Six. How many more to make ten?
Three?
Eight?
Five?
Nine?
Ten and some more. Look at the full ten-frame and the extra counters.
Ten and three more makes?
Ten and six more?
Twenty and four more?
Thirty and seven more?

If a child hesitates on 24 or 37, say the tens word slowly (twenty... four) and point to the tens and the ones in the picture. Do not move on until most children have answered; this idea is the lesson.
Answers: 4, 7, 2, 5, 1 then 13, 16, 24, 37. Children answer with fingers, hands or a whispered number. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Count the stars. Write how many. You may draw rings round groups to help.
Children count the stars and write the number on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Mei has 3 bundles of ten sticks and 4 single sticks. Ben has 34 sticks. Could they have the same number? Circle Yes or No. I know because ___.
Children write or draw their answer.
Keep your paper. Nobody shows it. We will check our own thinking later, at Talk time.
Thank you. We will come back to puzzle two in a few minutes.

Puzzle 1 answer: 24 stars. Puzzle 2 answer: yes, 3 tens and 4 ones is 34. Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who drew rings of ten, or who said 3 bundles is 30). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your hands are the teachers. Grab a handful of your small things, not the whole pile. Make bundles of ten. Count the bundles, then count the singles left over.
If you finish, try the what-if card: what if you open a bundle?
Round 1: each child grabs, bundles and counts. Tutor scans the cameras; a child who wants to may show their bundles to the camera. Nobody has to.
Tell me what you have. Say it like this: I have, how many tens, and how many ones.
Round two: show me! Use your tens bars and ones squares from the kit page. I call a number. You build it. I will tell you what it should look like, so you can check your own build.
Seventeen.
Children build 17, then give a thumbs-up when ready.
Check your own: one bar and seven squares.
Thirty.
Build 30.
Check your own: three bars and no squares.
Fifty-eight.
Build 58.
Check your own: five bars and eight squares.
One more. Ravi built thirty-five with 5 bars and 3 squares. Look at your kit. Is Ravi right?
Children check with their kit and answer by thumbs up or down, then say why. Answer: no, 5 bars and 3 squares is 53; thirty-five is 3 bars and 5 squares.
What did you notice? How many singles can be left over? Could you have ten singles left over? Why not?
If you have ten singles you can tie them into another bundle. So the singles left over are always nought to nine.
A child who counts bundles as ones (3 bundles and 4 singles is 7): hold up a real bundle and say, this one is worth ten. Count it: ten, twenty, thirty, then thirty-one, thirty-two.
A child with too few things: use the kit bars and squares for round 1 as well.

Main room only: no breakout rooms in this lesson, so you can see every camera. Pairs are optional: a grown-up may check the building. Building with the kit is for every child; the what-if card is for any child who wants it, and nobody is named.
@rec
Look. Ten single sticks. When I tie them together I have one bundle. One bundle is worth ten.
How many sticks are in one bundle?
Here are 3 bundles and 4 singles. I count the bundles in tens: ten, twenty, thirty. Then I count the singles: thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four. Thirty-four sticks.
I write it in two boxes. Tens: 3. Ones: 4. That makes 34. The left digit counts the tens. The right digit counts the ones.
Which digit tells me how many bundles?
Your turn. Write the number for each picture on your paper.
Children write three numbers.
Twenty-seven, forty, nineteen.
Look at forty. 4 bundles and no singles. We write a zero in the ones box. If we left it out, the 4 would look like 4 ones. The zero holds the place.
Twenty-six and sixty-two use the same digits. Which has more sticks, 26 or 62? How do you know?
The tens digit is worth more. 62 has 6 bundles. 26 has only 2 bundles. The order of the digits matters.
Sometimes you have lots of singles. Here are 2 bundles and 13 singles. Ten of the singles can tie into a new bundle. Now there are 3 bundles and 3 singles. Same sticks, 33 of them.
Why can we tie up ten singles? What is a bundle worth?
Quick-fire. I say a number. You tell me the tens and the ones. Forty-seven.
Sixty?
Nineteen?
Eighty-two?
Count together: tens, then ones: 10, 20, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34.

Key words to use every time: bundle (ten), single (one), tens digit, ones digit. Do not teach 'place value' as a term yet. Do not teach carrying. Keep ten singles making a bundle for the Think harder page.
If a child reads 34 as 43: ask them to build it with the kit bars and squares and say the tens first.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. A big jump for every ten, a small hop for every one. Thirty-four is three big jumps and four small hops.
Call 12, 25, 40, 31. Children jump the tens and hop the ones. Count the jumps and hops aloud together.
@rec
Page 1, Start here. Question 1: count the sticks and fill in the bundles, the singles and the number. Question 2: draw 3 bundles and 5 singles. Question 3: write the numbers.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Twenty-six. Thirty-five. Forty-two, seventy, nineteen, eighty-five. Mark your own page in another colour.
After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.
Page 2. Question 4: fill in tens and ones. Question 5: Ali has 47 sticks. Question 6: Kumar wrote 43. Is he right? Question 7: draw Ali's 6 bundles and Mei's 6 singles, and write each number.
Page 2, questions 4 to 7.
Five tens and eight ones. Four tens, no ones. Seven tens and one one. Four bundles, seven left over. Kumar should write thirty-four. Question 7: Ali has sixty, Mei has six.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time. Anything not finished is for home too.

Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page. If Start here took the whole time, say that pages 3 to 5 are for home, and keep the time.

Q2 (drawing): draw a bundle of ten as one long line and a single stick as a short line. Q4 (zero): ask how many singles are left over in 40. Q6: build 3 bundles and 4 singles with the kit, say the tens first. Q7: ask how much one bundle is worth.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. The grown-up can photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp. You then help in the open session in the next lesson. Never a private message to a child.

Think harder is for ideas taught today in a new setting. Go further is for mastery and extension. Do not announce who is on which page. Pairs are never split unless both children agree. Slow class: the workbook part needs about 31:50 against 28:00, so Start here may fill most of it. Take the extra minutes from the flex time, do not skip the answer slides, and say that pages 3 to 5 are for home.
@rec
Is 40 the same as 4? Circle Yes or No. Use bundles to explain: I know because ___.
Build 40 and 4 with your kit bars and squares. Which one has more?
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Mei has 3 bundles and 4 singles. Ben has 34 sticks. Yes! They have the same number, thirty-four.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.

Model answer: No. 40 is 4 bundles of ten and no singles. 4 is only 4 singles. 40 has more sticks. Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5.
E1. Look at the bundles and singles. How many sticks are there? E2. Thirty-seven equals how many tens and how many ones? E3. Write the number: seven tens and no ones.
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own.
Forty-eight. Three tens and seven ones. Seventy, and the zero is needed to show there are no ones.
Check your own ticket in a different colour. Well done. Put a star by each one you got right.

Nothing is collected or marked live. Children tick their own ticket. If many children miss one question, spend two minutes on it at the start of the next lesson, in the open session, no names. Do not read out any child's result.
@rec

Look-back. Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. If you like, tick one thing to try next time. You can pass. Nobody reads it out. If you tick 'I am still stuck', ask your grown-up to take a photo of this page after class and send it to our business WhatsApp. Then we will help you.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5.

Well done, inquirers. Next lesson is Number Words and the Number Line. Please have the number cards cut out from the kit pages, a small toy or a coin, and a pencil and paper. Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.
Optional, only if you are on time: what is the greatest number you can make with 9 bundles and 9 singles? And what happens if you add one more single?
Short think time, then take two answers.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

This is the standing buffer. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: 99; one more is ten bundles, which is called a hundred (next lessons). If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3) instead of rushing on.

slides.title: Bundles and Singles
slides.subtitle: Whole numbers: tens and ones

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Make bundles of ten, and use them to read and write numbers.

slides.note: Lesson 1 of Term 1, 90 minutes. Objective: read and write two-digit numbers as bundles of ten and single ones. Time plan: opening 0 to 4, warm-up 4 to 10, sneak-peek 10 to 14, explore 14 to 28, mini-lesson 28 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Tell the group the lesson is recorded (the tutor, the shared screen and any unmuted voice) and that a child may keep the camera off.

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Our lesson today

rows: Count in tens and show ten with fingers
Two puzzles. A guess is fine.

slides.note: Show this for about 20 seconds and name the phases only; do not read the table. Lesson 1 only: it introduces the routine every lesson follows.

slides.title: Four inquirer rules

items: Notice it. Look closely.
Test it. Try it with real things.
Explain why. Say how you know.
Mistakes help us. A guess is fine. You can pass.

blocks.head: RECORDING
items: We record the tutor, the screen and any voice that is unmuted. You may mute and keep your camera off.

slides.note: Read the four rules together. Say the recording notice in your own words: the platform records the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted; children's video is excluded; names are kept off the screen. A child or parent who does not wish to be heard can stay muted, and a camera can stay off. Then tell the shopkeeper story (47 pencils) and ask the group what a shopkeeper could do.

slides.title: Warm-up: count in tens

blocks.text: Clap on every number
Now count back from 100. Whisper, and big hands on 50!

slides.note: Count in tens to 100 with a clap on each number, then back to 0. This is a spiral review of skip counting in tens (holiday topic) and lets a new child join: they hear it before they say it.

slides.title: Fingers to ten

blocks.text: I show 6. How many more fingers make 10?

slides.note: Say each number; children show on their fingers how many more make ten. Answers: 6 needs 4, 3 needs 7, 8 needs 2, 5 needs 5, 9 needs 1. Hands up on camera is fine. No writing, no marks.

slides.title: Ten and some more

blocks.text: 10 and 3 more is ___

slides.note: Answers: 13, 16, 24, 37. Say the tens word slowly, then the ones: twenty... four. This is the bridge to bundles of ten and singles. Show 20 and 30 as two or three full ten-frames if a child is unsure.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Count the stars. Write how many.
You may draw rings round groups.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Mei has 3 bundles of ten sticks and 4 single sticks.
Ben has 34 sticks.
Could they have the same number? Circle Yes or No. I know because ___.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (24 stars) is an access question: any child can try it by counting or drawing rings. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson's key idea. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera: children keep their papers and check their own thinking at Talk time. There is no private chat and no board in front of the group. Answers: 24; yes (3 tens and 4 ones is 34). Do not reveal Puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list of who found it easy.

slides.title: Explore: grab and bundle

items: Grab a handful of small things. Not the whole pile.
Make bundles of ten: a hair tie, a cup, or a ring on paper.
Count the bundles. Count the singles left over.
Say: I have ___ tens and ___ ones.

blocks.head: WHAT IF?
items: What if you open a bundle? Can you show your number a different way?

slides.note: Round 1, about 4 minutes. Objects first, no writing yet. Children bundle in tens and count the singles. A child who wants to may show their bundles to the camera. The what-if card is available from the start so nobody waits: it previews the Think harder idea (opening a bundle), and no child is named for choosing it. A child with too few things can use the kit bars and squares.

slides.title: Show me!

blocks.text: Build each number with your tens bars and ones squares. Show a thumbs-up when it is built. Then check your own build.

slides.note: Round 2, about 3 minutes, main room. Call each number aloud and show it on the slide. Children build with the kit bars (tens) and squares (ones) and give a thumbs-up. Read the check line aloud so every child can check their own build; nobody holds anything up to the camera. Keep the builds to three: 17, 30 (the zero case) and 58. Answers: 17 is 1 bar and 7 squares; 30 is 3 bars; 58 is 5 bars and 8 squares. The picture of 23 is only an example. Camera tip: a child may tilt the screen so the table can be seen, but this is not required.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: How many singles can be left over?
Could you have ten singles left over? Why not?
Is it quicker to count 40 singles, or 4 tens?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key idea: the singles left over are always 0 to 9, because ten singles tie into another bundle. Counting in tens is quicker and easier to keep track of. Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up.

slides.title: Ten singles make a bundle

blocks.text: 10 singles = 1 bundle of ten

slides.note: Show ten single sticks, then tie them into one bundle. A bundle is worth ten. Ask: how many sticks are in one bundle? Answer: ten.

slides.title: Reading 34

blocks.text: 30 and 4 more is 34. The left digit counts the tens. The right digit counts the ones.

slides.note: Think aloud: count the bundles in tens (10, 20, 30) then the singles (31, 32, 33, 34). Write 3 in the tens box and 4 in the ones box. Ask: which digit tells me how many bundles? Answer: the left one, 3.

slides.title: Your turn: write the number

blocks.text: Write on your paper. Timer: 1 minute

slides.note: Each child writes on their own paper. Walk the cameras. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group.

slides.title: Check: write the number
slides.note: Answers: 27, 40, 19. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work.

slides.title: The zero holds the place

blocks.text: No singles, so the ones box has a 0. Without the 0, 4 would look like 4 ones.

slides.note: Zero ones means no singles. The zero is needed so the 4 stays in the tens place. A common slip is to write 4 for 4 tens.

slides.title: Same digits, different number

blocks.text: Which has more sticks? How do you know?

slides.note: 26 is 2 bundles and 6 singles. 62 is 6 bundles and 2 singles. 62 has more because the tens digit is worth more. The order of the digits matters. The Talk time question uses the zero case instead, so this idea is not repeated.

slides.title: Ten singles can tie up

blocks.text: 13 ones = 1 ten and 3 ones

slides.note: Show 2 bundles and 13 singles, then tie ten of the singles into a third bundle: 3 bundles and 3 singles. Both pictures are 33 sticks. This is the idea Think harder uses (5 tens and 14 ones). Keep it to about a minute: it is a worked example, not a new skill to drill.

slides.title: Count: tens, then ones

blocks.text: Say it together

slides.note: Count the 3 bundles then the 4 singles together. This is the same count as the explore. Keep it short.

slides.title: Jump the tens, hop the ones

blocks.text: A big jump for every ten. A small hop for every one.
34 is 3 big jumps and 4 small hops. Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call each number and have children jump the tens and hop the ones; count the jumps and hops aloud. No equipment. Keep it gentle for small spaces.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. Timer: 9 minutes

slides.note: Read questions 1 and 2 aloud. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children mark their own page in a different colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 7. Timer: 9 minutes

slides.note: Read question 6 aloud: it is a spot-the-mistake. Read question 7 aloud as well: draw Ali's and Mei's sticks. Children may draw bundles to decide.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Question 6 answer: no, Kumar should write 34, because 43 is 4 tens and 3 ones. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Question 7 answer: Ali has 60 and Mei has 6, because 6 tens is much more than 6 ones.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Our idea in a new setting
Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. Not finished? Pages 3 to 5 are for home too.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 4 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: TALK ABOUT IT
items: Is 40 the same as 4?

blocks.text: Use bundles to explain.
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: no. 40 is 4 bundles and no singles, and 4 is only 4 singles, so 40 has more. Repeat each child's answer in your own words for the recording.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: Yes! Mei and Ben can have the same number: 34.

slides.note: Reveal puzzle 2 now. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone's earlier answer.

slides.title: Exit ticket

blocks.text: On your own. No looking back. Timer: 3 minutes

slides.note: Children answer on page 5. Read E1, E2 and E3 aloud (the questions are on the slide). Children tick their own ticket against the next slide. Nobody holds paper to the camera and there is no private chat.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children check their own ticket in a different colour.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, a grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (the number is in the parent summary, never on a slide). You then help in the open session next lesson. Never a direct message to a child. The Next time I will try row is optional; at the start of the next lesson you may say to the whole group: today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: Number Words and the Number Line
Have ready: number cards, a small toy, pencil and paper.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (the look-back). Do not start anything new. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional menu slide and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: what if?

blocks.text: What is the greatest number you can make with 9 bundles and 9 singles?
What happens if you add one more single?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Answer: 99. One more single makes 10 singles, which tie into a tenth bundle: ten bundles. Ten tens have a name: a hundred (Lesson 2 onwards). Take two answers and move on.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: Add one more single. Does the ones digit always go up by one?
Write a mystery number puzzle for your grown-up
Show how to read 52 with bundles and singles

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

start.text: Write the place of each child.
start.hint: Start at the door. The first child is 1st.
start.solution: The child nearest the door is 1st, then 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th.

start.hint: Count the plates, then the cookies on one plate.

start.text: Look at the dots. The balls show 2 rows of 3.
start.hint: Count the rows and the dots in one row.
start.solution: 3 rows of 4 dots make 12 dots. Turning the page gives 4 rows of 3: also 12.

start.answer: 4 groups of 3 is 12; 6 groups of 5 is 30

investigation.title: Swap the numbers
investigation.first: Work out 2 × 5 and 5 × 2. Then try 3 × 4 and 4 × 3.
investigation.text: Always, sometimes or never: swapping the two numbers in a multiplication gives the same answer. Try 6 × 2. Write what you notice.
investigation.answer: Always (for the numbers tried): 10 and 10, 12 and 12, 12 and 12.
investigation.look_for: Several examples tried and a sentence about what stays the same.

talk.question: Is 40 the same as 4? Circle Yes or No. Use bundles to explain: I know because ___.
talk.answer: No. 40 is 4 bundles of ten and 0 singles. 4 is only 4 singles. 40 has more sticks, because the 4 in 40 counts bundles of ten.
talk.look_for: A reason that uses tens and ones (not just 'because 40 is bigger'). A child may say the zero holds the place.

parent.summary: We learned that a two-digit number is made of bundles of ten and single ones. Your child made bundles from real things, built numbers up to 58, and practised reading and writing numbers like 34 (3 tens and 4 ones) and 70 (7 tens and 0 ones). Tens and ones is familiar school work. Opening a bundle (5 tens and 14 ones is 6 tens and 4 ones) goes further, and is in Think harder and Go further.
words: bundle or ten: ten single things tied together
single or one: a thing on its own
tens digit: the left digit, it counts the bundles
ones digit: the right digit, it counts the singles
try_home: Bundle it: grab a handful of pasta, clips or buttons. Tie bundles of ten with hair ties or cups. Ask: how many tens and how many ones? Write the number together. Small things stay on the table, away from mouths and little brothers and sisters.
Show me: say a number up to 60 and let your child build it with bundles and singles. Swap roles and make a mistake on purpose for them to find.
Spot it: look at page numbers, lift buttons or door numbers. Ask: how many tens is that? Which digit tells you?
ask: Which digit tells how many bundles?
What if you opened a bundle?
parent.when_stuck: Please let your child use real things or draw bundles, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Please do not hurry or say it is easy. If the look-back page says 'I am still stuck', please photograph it and send it to our business WhatsApp (+65 9880 5962). Photos are kept up to 90 days.
parent.next: Next lesson: the stub has no next lesson.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones and to say why. This week: reading and writing two-digit numbers from bundles of ten and single ones.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones, to notice patterns and to say why.
parent.quote: A number is tens and ones. Ten singles tie into one bundle.

safeguarding: Small things stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears, and nothing is left where a younger brother or sister can reach it. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Use hair ties, cups or paper rings. No rubber bands: they can flick.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Nobody holds paper or a board up to the camera. Children tick their own work against the answer slide, answer together on a count of three, or show fingers or a thumb for a choice. There is no private chat.

Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted. Children may mute and keep their cameras off. A child's page is never shown.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. A grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp only; photos are kept for up to 90 days. The tutor then helps in the open session next lesson. No private messages to children, and no personal phones.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first.

Tell parents a week before: print workbook pages 1 to 6, cut out the kit page (page 6), find about 50 small things and 6 hair ties or cups. Small things stay away from mouths and from younger children.
Have the slides open and check the timer slide and the kit page are visible on screen share.
Check the recording captures the tutor and the shared screen. Children's video is excluded; any unmuted voice is recorded. Start the recording after the greeting, and avoid first names while it runs.

Tell parents plainly (it is on the parent page): Term 1 goes beyond the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose. Start here is explored in class with bundles and the kit; Think harder and Go further are optional stretch.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask 'How do you know?' and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: if you add one more single stick, the ones digit goes up by one. Is that always true? Try 23, 47 and 39 with your sticks or kit.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Try 23, 47 and 39 with one more single each. Is Mei always right?
menu.answer: Not always. 23 and 47 become 24 and 48. 39 plus one single makes ten singles, which tie into a new bundle: 40. It is true unless the ones digit is 9.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Pick a secret number. Write two clues about its tens and its ones, like: it has 4 bundles and the ones digit is 7. Give it to your grown-up to solve.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Write a mystery number puzzle with two clues for a grown-up to solve.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that the clues fit the secret number and fit only one number.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never seen bundles. Teach them how to read 52 using bundles and singles.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to read 52 with bundles and singles.
menu.answer: 52 is 5 bundles of ten and 2 singles. The left digit counts the bundles, the right digit counts the singles.
